oldtown: Town Hall Square and the House of the Blackheads

The heart of the Old Town: the square with the rebuilt façade of the House of the Blackheads, a 15th-century Gothic building, and the statue of Roland in front. All around are narrow medieval streets, courtyards and cafés.
peter: St Peter's Church and the view from the tower

The Gothic church whose very tall spire dominates the centre. A lift takes you up the tower to about 72 metres, from where you see all of Riga: the red roofs of the Old Town, the Daugava river and the new city.
dom: The largest medieval church in the Baltics, founded in 1211, with a wide, bright interior, a huge 19th-century organ and a cloister. The square in front is full of cafés and outdoor tables in the warm season.
tre: Three Brothers, Swedish Gate and the Cat House

A walk through Riga's oldest streets: the Three Brothers, three medieval houses side by side, the Swedish Gate, the only surviving gate of the walls, and the Cat House, with two black cats on the roof, near Livu Square.
freedom: Freedom Monument and the canal park

The symbol of independent Latvia, a 42-metre column topped by a woman holding up three stars. Behind it is the park along the city canal (Bastejkalns), with paths, little bridges and the National Opera.
market: One of Europe's largest covered markets, in five former German Zeppelin hangars from the First World War. Stalls of smoked fish, meat, dairy, rye bread and honey and, outside, fruit and vegetables. Great for tasting pīrāgi (bacon and onion buns) and picking up something to take home.
artn: A half-kilometre street with some of Europe's most incredible Art Nouveau buildings, mostly designed by Mikhail Eisenstein: façades with masks, sphinxes, peacocks and female figures. Riga has over 700 buildings in this style.
artnm: The restored apartment of the architect Konstantīns Pēkšēns, with original early-20th-century furniture, decoration, tiles and staircase. The best way to understand what Riga's middle-class homes were like.
occ: Museum of the Occupation of Latvia

The museum covers the period from 1940 to 1991, through the Soviet and Nazi occupations and the struggle for independence: documents, photos, objects and testimonies of those deported to Siberia. It explains a lot about today's Latvia.
lnma: A large early-20th-century neo-Baroque building with Latvian art from the 18th century to today: Symbolist painters, Soviet-era realism and modern works. It's quicker if you only want the permanent collection.
